messages.content: Write a page comparing a managed database service with running your own, for a technical audience choosing between them. Around 250 words.

output:
## Managed vs. Self-Hosted Databases

The choice rarely comes down to cost per gigabyte. It comes down to what you want your team spending time on.

A managed service (RDS, Cloud SQL, Atlas, PlanetScale) handles patching, backups, failover, and storage scaling. You get a dashboard, an API, and a bill that scales with usage. In exchange, you give up some control: you can't SSH into the box, tune every kernel parameter, or install arbitrary extensions. Most teams don't need to — but if you're running a workload with unusual requirements (custom extensions, specific replication topologies, exotic storage engines), the managed layer can become a wall instead of a floor.

Running your own database means real ownership: full access to configuration, the filesystem, the exact Postgres or MySQL build you want. It also means you own 3 a.m. disk-full alerts, replica lag during a failover, and the CVE that needs a patch this weekend. That's a real operational cost, and it doesn't show up on a pricing page.

The practical split: teams under roughly 10 engineers, or without dedicated database or SRE staff, come out ahead with managed services almost every time — the ops burden outweighs the control they'd gain. Larger organizations with dedicated infrastructure teams, unusual scale requirements, or strict data-residency rules that managed offerings can't satisfy have a stronger case for self-hosting.

A reasonable default: start managed. Move to self-hosted only when you can name the specific limitation forcing the change, not just the theoretical appeal of control.
